rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Research Background

Quantum biology is rapidly converging with device engineering, opening a field where biological macromolecules serve as quantum-active components in next-generation neuro-photonic and quantum-effect hardware. Recent findings indicate that quantum coherence, tunneling, and associated spin dynamics not only govern energy and charge flow in photosynthetic complexes and enzymes but can also be harnessed within solid-state-like architectures. This project targets ferritin, luciferase, and related proteins as naturally evolved, nanoscale platforms for device integration. Ferritin’s 24-mer nanocage—which encapsulates an iron-oxide core resembling semiconductor quantum dots—exhibits gateable electron transfer relevant to neuronal clusters such as the substantia nigra and locus coeruleus. By embedding these proteins into metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) geometries and hybrid photonic waveguides, the project explores spin-selective transport, photon-mediated signaling, and room-temperature quantum coherence—phenomena fundamental to neuromorphic computing. Success will provide bio-derived channel materials for low-power quantum sensors, neuromorphic synapses, and implantable optoelectronic interfaces, positioning protein-based MOSFETs at the forefront of neuro-photonic circuits and quantum biotechnology.


2. Research Objectives

① Fundamental Objectives

Investigate how various organic and protein materials (including enzymes, ferritin nanocages, and related biomolecules) function as active channels within MOSFET architectures. Systematically optimize device geometries to achieve high carrier mobility, high on/off ratios, minimal energy consumption, and fully tunable organic/bio-hybrid transistors.

② Scope Expansion

Pursue targeted protein engineering to enhance device performance, focusing on biocompatibility for biosensing applications and stimulus-responsive behavior (e.g., light or humidity gating) for environmentally adaptive electronics.

③ Analytical Methods

Employ ultrafast spectroscopy—specifically transient absorption spectroscopy—to resolve charge-transfer dynamics within protein-based MOSFET channels and correlate these dynamics with macroscopic device characteristics.



3. Expected Objectives

a. Quantum-activated biomolecular channels

By utilizing ferritin, luciferase, and related proteins as the intrinsic semiconductor layer in MOSFETs, this project integrates quantum biological functions with established micro/nano-fabrication techniques. Unlike conventional organic semiconductors, these proteins possess naturally evolved quantum-confined cores and spin-selective pathways, offering a previously unexplored route to room-temperature quantum coherence and spin-polarized charge transport in solid-state devices.

b. Integration of neuro-photonic devices

Embedding protein-based channels into photonic waveguides and neuromorphic circuit layouts enables simultaneous electrical, optical, and spin-based readouts. This multimodal platform can emulate synaptic behavior, paving the way for implantable neuro-photonic processors and ultra-low-power brain-computer interfaces—capabilities currently unattainable with inorganic or purely organic electronics.

c. Stimuli-responsive and biodegradable electronics

Rational protein engineering will introduce light-, humidity-, or pH-activated switches, yielding environmentally adaptive transistors that are inherently biocompatible and biodegradable. Such devices can be printed on flexible substrates for temporary biomedical diagnostics or eco-friendly IoT nodes, thereby addressing the growing problem of electronic waste.

1. Background

Wireless healthcare technologies are becoming increasingly important for patient monitoring, diagnosis, rehabilitation, and wearable medical systems. Antennas are a key component in these systems because they enable communication between sensors, medical devices, and external monitoring units. Healthcare antennas must be compact, lightweight, low-cost, safe for the human body, and able to operate reliably near lossy biological tissues. However, designing antennas for healthcare applications is challenging because the human body can detune the antenna, reduce radiation efficiency, and increase specific absorption rate (SAR). This project will investigate antenna designs suitable for wearable or body-centric healthcare applications, with a focus on improving performance, safety, and practical integration.


2. Main task

The main task of this FYP is to design, simulate, and evaluate a compact antenna for healthcare applications. The student will first review recent literature on wearable, implantable, and body-area-network antennas. Based on this review, suitable frequency bands such as ISM bands, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or 5G-related healthcare bands will be selected. The student will then design an antenna using electromagnetic simulation software such as CST, HFSS, or another suitable tool. The antenna performance will be quantified using parameters including reflection coefficient below −10 dB, bandwidth, gain, radiation efficiency, radiation pattern, and SAR. The effect of the human body or tissue-equivalent model will also be studied to understand antenna detuning and safety issues. Where possible, the design will be optimised to achieve compact size, stable operation, and SAR below standard safety limits.


3. Expected outcomes

By the end of the project, the student is expected to deliver a complete antenna design suitable for a healthcare-related application. The expected outcomes include a literature review, antenna geometry, simulation model, performance comparison, and technical discussion of the results. Quantified outcomes may include an operating frequency within the selected healthcare band, reflection coefficient below −10 dB, acceptable radiation efficiency, stable radiation pattern, and SAR compliance. The final report should clearly explain the design process, justify the selected parameters, compare the proposed design with existing work, and discuss possible future improvements such as fabrication, measurement, flexible substrates, or integration with wearable sensors.

rows.themePrerequisiteSkills:
I. Foundational

Knowledge


1. Optical Theory


Solid background in Geometrical Optics, including

Gaussian imaging formulas, paraxial optical systems, stops and aperture theory,

and aberration analysis, with the ability to design and analyze basic imaging

optical paths; Solid background in Physical Optics, with deep understanding of

core wave-optical concepts including interference, diffraction, and

polarization, capable of analyzing coherence and polarization effects in optical

systems; Solid background in Fourier Optics, mastering angular spectrum

propagation theory, spatial frequency analysis, the Fourier-transforming

property of lenses, and the interrelationship between Optical Transfer Function

(OTF) and Point Spread Function (PSF), with the ability to model and analyze

imaging systems using Fourier methods.

2. Software Proficiency


Proficiency in Matlab: capable of independently

writing numerical simulation programs for optical field propagation

calculations (e.g., angular spectrum method, Fresnel diffraction integral),

phase profile generation, image processing and quality assessment, and data

visualization; Proficiency in Zemax: capable of building imaging optical paths

in sequential mode, setting merit functions for phase profile optimization of

lenses/metasurfaces, and performing aberration analysis and tolerance analysis;

Proficiency in CST Studio Suite: capable of building periodic electromagnetic

simulation models, setting boundary conditions and excitation sources, executing

frequency-domain/time-domain solver simulations, performing parameter sweeps,

extracting S-parameters, and obtaining amplitude and phase response data of

unit cells.

3. Metasurface

Fundamentals


Understanding of basic operating principles of

metasurfaces, including the Generalized Snell's Law, Pancharatnam-Berry (P-B)

phase modulation mechanism, and Propagation Phase modulation mechanism; Understanding

of typical applications of metasurfaces in wavefront shaping, beam steering,

and lens imaging; Understanding of the mapping relationship between geometric

parameters (height, diameter, period, duty cycle) of metasurface unit

structures (e.g., nanopillars, nanofins, split-ring resonators) and their

optical responses (amplitude and phase).

II. Design Workflow


This project follows a complete R&D pipeline

of "theoretical design → numerical simulation → iterative optimization → experimental

fabrication → system

validation." The specific workflow is as follows:

Step 1: System Parameter

Pre-Design


Based on the application requirements of

high-resolution projection displays, determine the core design parameters of

the system, including: operating wavelength (λ, e.g., 532 nm green or 635 nm

red), target resolution (e.g., from 128×128 to 256×256 pixels), imaging geometry

(metasurface effective aperture and pixel size), projection distance (50–200

mm), resolution enhancement factor (2×2 or 3×3 stitching scheme), and

translation stepping precision (sub-pixel level). The output parameters of this

step serve as the boundary conditions for all subsequent design and simulation

stages.

Step 2: Metasurface Phase

Profile Optimization (Zemax)


Import the system parameters determined in Step 1

into Zemax to establish a complete projection optical model. Using minimization

of the Point Spread Function (PSF), minimization of wavefront error, or

maximization of the Modulation Transfer Function (MTF) as the optimization

goal, employ Zemax's sequential mode optimization functions to compute the

optimal phase profile φ(x, y) required for the metasurface. This phase profile

determines how the metasurface modulates the incident wavefront and is the core

element for achieving high-quality projection imaging.

Step 3: Unit Cell

Electromagnetic Simulation and Parameter Sweep (CST)


Build an electromagnetic simulation model of the

basic metasurface unit cell in CST Studio Suite. Design the unit cell geometry

(e.g., cylindrical nanopillars, square nanopillars), select substrate material

(e.g., SiO₂ or glass) and unit cell material (e.g., a-Si, TiO₂, or Si₃N₄). Set

periodic boundary conditions and plane-wave excitation, perform comprehensive

parameter sweeps over geometric parameters (height, diameter/side length,

period), and calculate the amplitude transmittance and phase delay for each

combination of geometric parameters. Finally, establish a complete

"structural parameters ↔ optical response" Look-Up Table (LUT) to

provide data support for subsequent unit cell arrangement.

Step 4: Inverse Mapping from

Phase Profile to Unit Cell Distribution and Layout Generation


Discretize and sample the continuous phase profile

φ(x, y) obtained in Step 2 according to the metasurface pixel grid. For each

discrete pixel position, search the LUT established in Step 3 to find the unit

cell geometric parameters whose phase value most closely matches the target and

whose amplitude transmittance is maximized, completing the inverse mapping from

phase to structure. Generate the complete metasurface layout based on the

matching results, exporting as a standardized GDSII format file or a custom

matrix format file for subsequent fabrication.

Step 5: Optical Propagation

Simulation and Image Reconstruction (Matlab)


Based on Fourier optics and angular spectrum

propagation theory, establish a numerical model of optical field propagation

through the metasurface in Matlab. Input the metasurface phase arrangement

generated in Step 4, simulate the outgoing optical field after metasurface

modulation and the imaging field distribution on the projection screen.

Simulate the sub-image projection results at different translational positions

of the metasurface (e.g., 4 positions in a 2×2 grid or 9 positions in a 3×3

grid), and use image stitching and super-resolution reconstruction algorithms

to fuse multiple low-resolution sub-frames into a single high-resolution image.

Calculate quality metrics of the reconstructed image including PSF, MTF,

contrast ratio, and SNR.

Step 6: Simulation Result

Analysis and Iterative Optimization


Perform a point-by-point comparative analysis between

the simulation outputs from Step 5 and the quantitative targets set in Step 1.

If any metric fails to meet the target, trace the error sources (possible

sources include phase discretization error, unit cell amplitude non-uniformity,

stitching misalignment error, insufficient diffraction efficiency, etc.) and

return to Step 2, Step 3, or Step 5 for targeted adjustments. Complete at least

two rounds of iterative optimization until all performance indicators satisfy

the design requirements.

Step 7: Metasurface Sample

Fabrication


Based on the GDSII layout file output from Step 4,

proceed with micro/nano fabrication either in-house or through a foundry

service. A typical process flow includes: substrate cleaning → EBL resist spin-coating

→ electron-beam lithography

(EBL) → development → reactive ion etching

(RIE) → resist stripping. After

fabrication, characterize the sample morphology using scanning electron

microscopy (SEM) to confirm that the dimensions and morphology of the unit

structures are consistent with the design layout.

Step 8: Experimental

Platform Construction and System Validation


Build a complete optical

testing platform comprising: a laser source (wavelength consistent with design)

→ beam expansion and collimation system → metasurface sample (mounted on a high-precision

piezoelectric translation stage) → projection screen → CMOS image acquisition camera. Write stage control and image

acquisition synchronization programs. According to the translation scheme

determined in Step 1, step the stage sequentially and capture low-resolution

sub-images at each position. Input the captured sub-image sequence into the

image stitching and reconstruction algorithm to obtain the final high-resolution

projected image. Compare the measured results (resolution, contrast ratio, MTF,

etc.) with simulation predictions to validate the correctness of the design and

analyze sources of experimental error.
rows.themeProjectDescription:
I. Introduction


Conventional projection display technologies have long relied

on spatial light modulators such as digital micromirror devices (DMDs) and

liquid crystal on silicon (LCoS) panels, which modulate incident light pixel by

pixel to project images. As display resolutions advance from high-definition

toward 4K, 8K, and beyond, these technologies face increasingly severe

challenges: the continuous scaling of pixel size is not only constrained by the

physical limits of semiconductor manufacturing processes, but also leads to

reduced optical efficiency, increased thermal dissipation issues, and

drastically higher driving circuit complexity. Breaking through the resolution

bottleneck while maintaining system compactness and low cost has therefore become

a critical scientific challenge in the field of projection displays.

Metasurfaces—two-dimensional arrays of subwavelength unit

structures functioning as artificial electromagnetic interfaces—offer flexible

control over the amplitude, phase, and polarization of optical fields at

subwavelength scales, providing a brand-new platform for next-generation

ultra-thin projection optical systems. However, the space-bandwidth product of

a single metasurface is fundamentally limited by its physical pixel count, and

relying solely on fabrication process improvements to increase pixel density

faces the same trade-offs between cost and precision.

To address these challenges, this project proposes an

innovative scheme of "translationally reconfigurable metasurfaces":

by translating the metasurface with high-precision mechanical stages, multiple

frames of low-resolution sub-images are sequentially projected at different

spatial positions. Through sub-pixel image stitching and super-resolution

reconstruction algorithms, these sub-frames are fused into a single

high-resolution image. The core philosophy of this approach is "trading

time for space"—sacrificing temporal sampling to achieve spatial

resolution beyond the physical pixel limit, without requiring any advancement

in fabrication technology. This strategy synergistically integrates the

subwavelength light-field modulation capability of metasurfaces, the

multi-frame fusion theory of computational imaging, and precision displacement

control techniques, opening up a new pathway for developing ultra-compact,

low-cost, and reconfigurable high-resolution projection systems. This research

aims to establish a complete technical framework encompassing theoretical

design, simulation optimization, and experimental validation, thereby advancing

the practical application of reconfigurable metasurfaces in dynamic displays.

II. Main Task


The primary tasks of this project span the entire chain of

"design—simulation—fabrication—validation," and specifically include

the following core components: System parameter design and quantitative

specification: Define key parameters including operating wavelength, target

resolution, projection distance, and field of view based on application

requirements. Determine the resolution enhancement factor (target: 4×

enhancement, from 128×128 to 256×256 pixels) and the corresponding translation

stepping scheme.

Metasurface phase profile optimization: Build a projection

optical model in Zemax based on system parameters, and solve for the optimal

phase profile of the metasurface by minimizing the point spread function and

wavefront error.

Unit cell electromagnetic simulation and database construction:

Establish the basic unit cell model of the metasurface in CST, perform

parameter sweeps to obtain amplitude transmittance and phase delay data for

varying geometric dimensions, and construct a comprehensive

"structure—optical response" lookup table.

Inverse mapping from phase to structure and layout

generation: Discretize the theoretically optimized phase profile, match each

pixel to the nearest available unit structure from the database, and generate a

fabricable metasurface layout file.

Numerical simulation of optical propagation and image

reconstruction: Based on Fourier optics and angular spectrum propagation

theory, simulate the projected imaging results of the metasurface at each

translational position using Matlab, reconstruct the high-resolution image via

multi-frame stitching algorithms, and compute quality metrics such as MTF and

contrast ratio.

Iterative optimization: Based on simulation feedback,

iteratively refine the phase profile, unit cell structures, and stitching

algorithms to ensure all performance specifications meet the design targets.

Metasurface sample fabrication: Fabricate the metasurface

sample on transparent substrates using micro/nano-fabrication processes

including electron-beam lithography and reactive ion etching, followed by

scanning electron microscopy characterization.

Experimental platform construction and system validation:

Build an optical testing system comprising a laser source, beam collimation

optics, a high-precision piezoelectric translation stage, and a CMOS camera.

Conduct actual translation-projection imaging experiments to validate the

consistency between simulation results and real-system performance.

III. Expected Results


The core focus of this research lies in the functional

realization and performance validation of translationally reconfigurable

metasurface projection displays, with technical significance manifested in the

following aspects: In terms of imaging resolution, through multi-frame

sub-pixel translational stitching, the spatial resolution of the projected

image is expected to be enhanced by a factor of 4 (2×2 stitching) or 9 (3×3

stitching) relative to the physical pixel count, thereby demonstrating the

feasibility and effectiveness of the "trading time for space"

strategy in metasurface-based display systems. In terms of imaging quality, the

reconstructed images are expected to achieve a contrast ratio exceeding 10:1

and a modulation transfer function no lower than 0.3 at the target resolution,

ensuring clear edges and rich fine details.

In terms of device performance, the designed metasurface unit

structures are expected to exhibit transmittance of no less than 60% and full

2π phase coverage, providing the foundation for high-efficiency light-field

modulation. In terms of system integration, a complete technical workflow

spanning theoretical design (Zemax + CST + Matlab), micro/nano fabrication, and

optical testing will be established, laying the groundwork for future system

miniaturization and dynamic reconfiguration.

Building upon these research outcomes, the translationally

reconfigurable metasurface projection technology holds promise for future

applications in the following scenarios: (1) ultra-compact portable projectors,

leveraging the ultra-thin planar nature of metasurfaces to dramatically reduce

projection engine volume, suitable for wearable displays and mobile smart

devices; (2) augmented reality displays, serving as compact light engines for

high-resolution image projection; (3) computational imaging systems, combined

with the dynamic tunability of reconfigurable metasurfaces to achieve

switchable resolution and field-of-view adaptive projection displays. The

successful implementation of this project will provide critical theoretical

foundations and experimental support for the interdisciplinary convergence of

novel flat-panel display technologies and dynamic metasurface modulation

techniques.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
（1）Background

Piezoelectric materials are core functional components in micro-energy harvesting, flexible sensors, MEMS actuators and wearable electronic devices, showing great application value in industrial monitoring and consumer electronics. Traditional bulk piezoelectric materials are limited by high brittleness and poor shape adaptability, while piezoelectric composites prepared by liquid polymer matrix curing have the advantages of low cost, simple process, good flexibility and customizable morphology. Currently, PZT (lead zirconate titanate) is the most widely used piezoelectric filler with outstanding piezoelectric performance; BTO (barium titanate) is a representative lead-free piezoelectric material with excellent environmental compatibility; ZnO (zinc oxide) has the characteristics of low cost, easy synthesis and stable chemical properties. However, there is still a lack of systematic comparative study on the piezoelectric properties of these three materials under completely consistent preparation and polarization conditions in the same liquid matrix system. This project carries out controlled variable experiments to fill this research gap and provide data reference for the selection of piezoelectric fillers in flexible composite systems.

（2）Main Task

1. Prepare three groups of piezoelectric composite samples by doping PZT, BTO and ZnO particles into the same liquid epoxy resin matrix respectively, with strictly consistent filler mass fraction, mixing process, curing temperature and curing time.

2. Optimize the polarization process parameters (polarization electric field strength, polarization temperature and holding time), and perform high-voltage polarization treatment on all cured samples under unified conditions.

3. Test and characterize key performance parameters of the three samples, including piezoelectric strain constant d33, relative dielectric constant, dielectric loss, electromechanical coupling coefficient and cycle stability of piezoelectric response.

4. Conduct comparative analysis on the performance differences of the three composites, and explain the internal mechanism combined with microstructure characterization results.

（3）Expected Outcomes

1. Obtain complete and reliable comparative data of piezoelectric and dielectric properties for PZT, BTO and ZnO polymer matrix composites.

2. Clarify the performance advantages, limitations and applicable scenarios of the three piezoelectric fillers in liquid curing matrix systems.

3. Summarize a set of standardized preparation and polarization process scheme for liquid-based piezoelectric composite materials.

4. Complete a full graduation design thesis containing complete experimental data, mechanism analysis and research conclusions, meeting the academic requirements of the final year project.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background Mobile banking apps increasingly use face recognition to authenticate users. A face check is only safe if the system can confirm the camera is seeing a live person rather than a photo, a replayed video, or a mask — a problem known as face liveness detection. As phone cameras and consumer media tools improve, simple spoofing attempts (printed photos, screen replays) are easy to attempt, so banking apps need a liveness layer that is accurate, fast on ordinary phones, privacy-respecting, and aligned with recognised testing standards. This is a civilian, consumer-facing anti-fraud problem built entirely on publicly available datasets, open-source tools, and published methods.

2. Main task Students will design, implement, and evaluate a complete face-liveness pipeline for a banking-style mobile app, from camera input to a live/not-live decision, with on-device, privacy-by-design operation. The theme is engineering-led: each student creates and justifies design decisions, evaluates alternatives, and validates performance against recognised benchmarks (e.g. the iBeta / ISO/IEC 30107-3 presentation-attack-detection testing philosophy) rather than only applying an off-the-shelf model.

3. Expected outcomes A working, documented liveness-detection prototype (model + mobile integration), a reproducible evaluation harness, measured accuracy/latency/model-size trade-offs across phones, and a design rationale covering security-versus-usability, privacy, and standards compliance.

Division of labour (independent objectives, minimal overlap):

  • S1 — Mobile face detection & preprocessing front-end. Design a fast, robust face-detection and alignment stage (OpenCV/MediaPipe) tuned for low-power phones; characterise latency vs accuracy.
  • S2 — Liveness classification model. Design and train a CNN live/not-live classifier on public datasets (e.g. CASIA-FASD, Replay-Attack, OULU-NPU); justify architecture choices and evaluate.
  • S3 — Robustness to print & replay attacks. Engineer texture/frequency/motion features to separate live faces from 2-D photo and screen-replay attempts; evaluate detection performance.
  • S4 — Model compression for deployment. Apply quantisation, pruning, and distillation for TensorFlow Lite; measure model-size vs accuracy trade-offs.
  • S5 — Cross-device performance evaluation. Build a test harness assessing consistency across phone types, camera qualities, and OSs, with uncertainty analysis.
  • S6 — Generalisation evaluation framework. Design a cross-dataset protocol to test how well the system handles attack types unseen during training.
  • S7 — Banking app integration & user experience. Build the front-end app (React Native/Flutter) integrating the model; tune the security threshold (FAR/FRR) against usability.
  • S8 — Standards, privacy & compliance-by-design. Map the system to iBeta Level 2 / ISO/IEC 30107 testing and GDPR privacy-by-design (on-device inference, data minimisation); analyse societal, ethical, and commercial impact.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Emerging technologies such as Virtual Reality (VR), Extended Reality (XR), Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), and multimodal analytics are transforming the future of education and professional training. Intelligent immersive learning environments can provide personalised, interactive, and emotionally responsive learning experiences that enhance learner engagement, motivation, and knowledge retention. This project theme focuses on the design and development of AI-powered immersive learning systems that integrate virtual environments, conversational AI, emotion and engagement recognition, and real-time learning analytics. Students will develop a platform that improves human learning experiences while gaining hands-on experience in artificial intelligence, computer vision, signal processing, human-computer interaction, and immersive technologies.


Project 1: Generative AI for 360° Immersive Learning Environment Creation

This project explores the use of Generative AI techniques to automatically create immersive 360° learning environments for VR/XR applications. Students will develop a workflow for generating educational scenes from text prompts and integrating them into interactive immersive learning experiences.


Project 2: Real-Time Gaze Tracking and Learning Analytics in Immersive Environments

This project investigates the use of eye-tracking technologies to analyse learner attention, engagement, and interaction behaviour in immersive environments. The developed system will provide real-time learning analytics and adaptive feedback to enhance the learning experience.


Project 3: Conversational AI Agents for Intelligent and Collaborative Immersive Learning

This project focuses on integrating conversational AI agents into immersive learning environments to provide personalised tutoring, real-time feedback, and interactive guidance. The intelligent agent will support learners through natural language interaction and context-aware educational assistance.


Project 4: Emotion and Engagement Recognition for Emotionally Intelligent Immersive Learning

This project aims to develop an emotionally intelligent immersive learning system that recognises learners' emotional and engagement states using multimodal sensing and AI techniques. The recognised emotional state will be used to adapt learning content, interaction style, or AI tutor behaviour in real time.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
With the rapid development of integrated energy systems, accurate load forecasting is the key to optimizing energy scheduling, improving energy utilization efficiency and ensuring system stable operation. Traditional load forecasting methods have poor adaptability to the nonlinear and fluctuating characteristics of multi‑energy loads. Artificial intelligence algorithms have strong nonlinear fitting ability, which can effectively mine the correlation of load data and improve the accuracy of load forecasting, so it is suitable for the load forecasting research of integrated energy systems.


The main tasks are as follows:


1. Collect and preprocess the historical load data of integrated energy system, including data cleaning, normalization and feature selection;


2. Analyze the influencing factors of heating, power and hydrogen load in integrated energy system;


3. Design and build an artificial intelligence‑based load forecasting model for integrated energy system;


4. Train, optimize and test the forecasting model to improve the forecasting accuracy and generalization ability;


5. Compare and analyze the performance of the proposed model with traditional forecasting methods to verify its effectiveness.


Expected results are as follows:


1. An effective artificial intelligence load forecasting model suitable for integrated energy system;


2. A graduation thesis that systematically summarizes the research process, methods and research conclusions of load forecasting of integrated energy system based on artificial intelligence.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
With the rapid development of UAV technology, path planning has become a core issue in UAV applications. Traditional path planning algorithms have limitations in complex dynamic environments, such as poor adaptability and low efficiency. Reinforcement learning, as a branch of artificial intelligence, can enable UAVs to learn optimal navigation strategies through continuous interaction with the environment, which provides a new solution for solving UAV path planning problems in complex scenarios.


The main tasks are as follows:


1) Build a simulation environment for UAV path planning, including obstacle setting and dynamic scenario construction.


2) Design and implement a reinforcement learning algorithm (such as DQN or PPO) for UAV path planning.


3)Train and optimize the model to improve the UAV's ability to avoid obstacles and find the optimal path.


4) Conduct comparative experiments with traditional path planning algorithms to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.


Expected results are as follows:


1) A set of reinforcement learning-based UAV path planning algorithms that can adapt to complex dynamic environments.


2) A graduation thesis summarizing the research process and results.

This project theme focuses on developing Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven solutions for detecting, monitoring, and analyzing subsea environments, particularly in relation to marine pollution (e.g., plastic and waste) and marine life monitoring. With the growing demand for environmental sustainability and underwater ecosystem protection, students will explore applications such as object detection, marine debris identification, and marine life classification using AI techniques.


  1. AI-Based Detection of Marine Plastic Waste in Underwater Images: This project uses AI/computer vision to detect plastic waste such as bottles, bags, and wrappers in underwater images.It helps support marine pollution monitoring by automatically identifying harmful plastic materials in subsea environments.
  2. Marine Debris Classification Using Artificial Intelligence: This project focuses on classifying different types of marine debris, such as plastic, metal, glass, fishing gear, and general waste. It can help researchers understand the type and quantity of pollution present in underwater ecosystems.
  3. AI-Based Jellyfish Species Classification for Subsea Monitoring: This project uses image classification techniques to identify different jellyfish species from underwater images.It is useful for monitoring jellyfish populations, studying marine biodiversity, and detecting species changes in the ocean.
  4. Snail Image Classification Using Artificial Intelligence: This project applies AI models to classify different snail species or snail images based on visual features. It can support biodiversity studies and help monitor aquatic or marine snail populations in environmental research.
  5. Marine Shell and Snail Shell Recognition Using Artificial Intelligence: This project uses deep learning to recognize and classify marine shells and snail shells from image datasets.It can help with species identification, marine biodiversity documentation, and ecological monitoring.
  6. Underwater Image Enhancement for Improving Marine Object Detection: This project improves the quality of underwater images affected by poor lighting, blur, haze, or colour distortion. Enhanced images can improve the accuracy of AI models used for detecting marine life, plants, and pollution.
  7. AI Dashboard for Monitoring Marine Pollution and Marine Life from Underwater Images: This project develops a dashboard to display AI results such as detected waste, marine life types, confidence scores, and image summaries. It helps users visualize subsea monitoring data and understand environmental conditions more easily.
  8. AI-Based Seagrass Detection and Classification for Marine Ecosystem Monitoring: This project uses AI to detect and classify seagrass or underwater plants from marine images. Seagrass is important because it provides habitat for marine life, improves water quality, and acts as an indicator of ecosystem health.

1. Background

Speech keyword recognition is an important task in human-computer interaction, smart devices, voice control systems, and edge intelligence applications. Compared with full automatic speech recognition, keyword recognition focuses on detecting a limited set of predefined commands, such as “yes”, “no”, “stop”, or “go”, which makes it suitable for low-power and real-time systems. With the development of deep learning, neural-network-based methods have achieved significantly better recognition performance than traditional hand-crafted feature and template-matching approaches. However, many deep learning models still suffer from high computational cost and large parameter size, which may limit their deployment on resource-constrained devices. Therefore, this project aims to study and implement a deep learning-based speech keyword recognition method with a balance between recognition accuracy and model efficiency.


2. Main Task

The main task of this project is to design, train, and evaluate a speech keyword recognition model based on deep learning. The student is expected to complete audio data preprocessing, including waveform loading, resampling, normalization, and feature extraction using Mel-spectrogram or MFCC features. A baseline neural network, such as CNN, CRNN, or a lightweight deep learning model, will be implemented using Python and PyTorch or TensorFlow. The model will be trained and tested on a public speech keyword dataset, such as Google Speech Commands. The project should compare at least two model structures or settings, and analyze their performance in terms of recognition accuracy, parameter size, computational complexity, and inference time.


3. Expected Outcomes

The expected outcome is a complete deep learning-based speech keyword recognition system. The target is to achieve a recognition accuracy of over 90% on a standard test set for selected keywords. The student is also expected to complete a well-structured FYP report, source code, trained model files, and a simple demonstration program that can recognize speech commands from audio samples.

1. Background

Precision agriculture leverages IoT technologies to monitor environmental conditions and optimise farming practices. With the growing demand for sustainable food production, data-driven techniques can help farmers make timely and resource-efficient decisions. This theme project brings together four students to design an end-to-end precision agriculture system that integrates environmental sensing, automation, plant/pest monitoring, and cloud-based analytics.

The work is organised as a single coherent theme, but each student owns an independent design problem with its own literature review, design, implementation, and testing. The subsystems communicate through a shared, agreed interface so that the individual contributions combine into one working prototype, while each remains assessable as a stand-alone engineering design. The system is intended for civilian, small-scale farm use only and is built entirely from published, open-domain techniques and components.

2. Main Task

Develop and prototype a modular IoT system for a small-scale farm setup. The system consists of distributed sensing and monitoring nodes, an automated irrigation controller, a communication backbone, and a combined data platform that provides visualisation, alerting, and recommendations. The team will simulate or implement field conditions and test the system's effectiveness in monitoring and optimising crop management. Each of the four students delivers one subsystem and demonstrates how it meets a defined combination of user, environmental, and operational needs, including reliability, power, cost, and safety in an outdoor farm context.

3. Expected Outcomes

• Distributed sensing covering soil and weather conditions.

• Camera/sensor-based monitoring of plant health and pest presence.

• Automated, sensor-driven irrigation control.

• A combined data platform: ingestion, storage, live dashboard, alerting, and recommendations.

• Documentation, test results, and recommendations based on field simulation or lab testing.

4. Individual Work Directions and Objectives

The original concept has been consolidated into four independent student roles. The soil and weather units are combined into a single Environmental Sensing Node; the crop-imaging and pest-detection units are combined into a single Crop Health & Pest Monitoring Node; and the dashboard and analytics functions are combined into a single Data Platform owning the full backbone from ingestion through to recommendations. Each role below is a distinct design problem with minimal overlap.


Student 1 — Environmental Sensing Node (Soil & Weather)

Literature Review: Study soil moisture and temperature sensing techniques together with low-cost weather station designs, and their combined relevance to irrigation and crop planning.

System Design: Select suitable sensors for soil moisture, soil temperature, rainfall, light, humidity, and air temperature, and integrate them with a single microcontroller-based node, addressing weatherproofing and power.

Implementation: Build a node that collects soil and weather data and transmits it wirelessly to the data platform at set intervals.

Testing: Evaluate sensor accuracy across varying soil and weather conditions (wet/dry, temperature range) and validate weather readings against reference datasets or calibrated instruments.


Student 2 — Smart Irrigation Controller

Literature Review: Explore irrigation scheduling techniques and sensor-based automation strategies.

System Design: Develop control logic that uses incoming soil and weather data to decide when to activate irrigation valves, defining clear, safe actuation rules.

Implementation: Create a controller that interfaces with solenoids or pumps and acts on data received from the sensing node and commands from the platform.

Testing: Simulate different soil-moisture scenarios and verify that irrigation behaviour responds correctly and safely.


Student 3 — Crop Health & Pest Monitoring Node

Literature Review: Investigate imaging methods for plant health monitoring and IoT-based pest detection methods, comparing camera-based and sensor-based approaches.

System Design: Use an embedded camera (and, where suitable, a light trap with sensors) to capture periodic images and detect signs of plant stress and insect presence.

Implementation: Implement image- or signal-based analysis to flag unhealthy plants and classify pest presence, and report results to the data platform.

Testing: Compare outputs across healthy versus stressed plant setups and simulated or lab-captured pest specimens to assess detection reliability.


Student 4 — Data Platform: Integration, Monitoring & Analytics

Literature Review: Study dashboard UX/UI approaches and suitable frameworks (e.g., Node-RED, Flask); data ingestion and time-series storage for heterogeneous sensor streams; methods for handling input-data uncertainty; and simple, interpretable data-analysis/ML approaches in farming (e.g., regression, threshold-based rules).

System Design: Design a pub/sub ingestion layer (e.g., MQTT) with a defined API that all nodes publish to, plus time-series storage; a live dashboard with charts, alerts (using hysteresis/debouncing to avoid alert storms) and remote access; offline-first store-and-forward for poor rural connectivity; a command path to the irrigation controller with acknowledgement and failure handling; and recommendation logic that converts combined data into irrigation, fertilisation, or pest-control guidance. Remote access uses standard published mechanisms (TLS, token-based auth) — applying established practice, not developing new encryption.

Implementation: Build the ingestion layer, storage, dashboard interface, alerting, and a rule-based or predictive recommendation engine as one integrated platform serving the three field subsystems.

Testing: Measure real-time update latency; test behaviour under missing, late, out-of-order, and conflicting readings and simulated node dropouts; assess performance as node count scales; and compare the system's recommendations against known optimal actions on simulated datasets.


5. Integration and Independence

To satisfy the requirement that each project be independent with minimal overlap, the four students agree a shared data and communication interface early in the project but design and build their own subsystems separately. The three field subsystems (Students 1-3) each design against that interface, while Student 4 owns the platform that receives, stores, presents, and acts on their data. Each subsystem can be tested in isolation against the agreed interface, and the team integrates them into a single demonstrable prototype for the final defence. This lets every student evidence their own design decisions, analysis of input-data uncertainty, and consideration of the wider engineering context, while the combined system shows the full precision-agriculture workflow from sensing through to recommendation.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background: With the scaling of advanced semiconductor process nodes, electrostatic discharge (ESD) protection for integrated circuit ports faces severe challenges. In some application scenarios, due to the possibility of pin voltages being lower than ground potential, there is an urgent need for bipolar devices that can provide effective clamping protection in both positive and negative directions. Traditional bidirectional SCR structures often suffer from the problem of excessively low holding voltage. In recent years, the holding voltage of devices has been effectively improved by introducing self-biased gates and additional implantation regions. The latest research further shows that the adoption of a three-implantation region design including an N-drift region can significantly improve current distribution and reduce dynamic resistance in high-voltage applications. However, how to balance various electrical indicators and the thermal stability degradation mechanism of the device in the extreme high-temperature environment from 300K to 500K remain the key core difficulties in current protection design. This project aims to reveal the complex multi-physics coupling mechanism inside the new bidirectional SCR through numerical simulation.


2. Main task: 1. Literature analysis and physical mechanism combing: Systematically study core literature to clarify the underlying structural evolution logic and feedback physical essence of bidirectional SCR devices from "introducing P+ regions to reduce trigger voltage", "self-biased gates to improve holding voltage" to "N-drift three-implantation regions to reduce dynamic resistance". 2. Two-dimensional TCAD device modeling and benchmark transient simulation: Use the Sentaurus TCAD simulation platform to construct a two-dimensional cross-sectional model of the bidirectional SCR including P+ bridge regions, self-biased gates, and N-drift regions. Reasonably configure carrier mobility, avalanche breakdown, and recombination models. Under TLP pulse (10ns rising edge) transient excitation, obtain transient and quasi-static characteristic curves and key physical parameters such as internal electric field and carrier concentration. 3. Joint regulation of key structural parameters and law induction (core task): Design multi-variable orthogonal scanning experiments for the core design variables in the literature. Systematically explore the joint constraints of different structural size combinations on trigger voltage, holding voltage, and secondary breakdown current, and optimize the design window as much as possible. 4. Thermal stability and internal field evolution analysis under extreme working conditions (core task): Introduce the ambient temperature gradient from 300K to 500K as the core variable. Carry out thermodynamics and electrical simulations, deeply extract and compare the collision ionization rate, carrier recombination rate, and electrostatic potential distribution inside the device at different temperatures. Analyze the influence of high temperature on key parameters such as trigger voltage and holding voltage.


3. Expected outcomes: 1. Establishment of simulation engineering library: Submit a set of structurally complete and code-standard new bidirectional SCR device Sentaurus TCAD simulation engineering file libraries, covering the complete process from device construction to TLP transient simulation. 2. Multidimensional feature data visualization analysis: Proficiency in using SVisual post-processing tools to accurately read simulation output data files. Draw comparative I-V characteristic curves under multiple sets of key variables, as well as two-dimensional color contour maps of internal electric field and carrier concentration, and be able to analyze and explain from the underlying physical mechanism. 3. Construct an electro-thermal coupling simulation model for a wide temperature range (300K-500K), accurately quantify the thermal degradation law of bidirectional SCR trigger characteristics and holding voltage; and accurately define the thermal failure boundary of the device, providing rigorous theoretical support and optimization criteria for the anti-thermal degradation design of high-reliability ESD protection structures. 4. Standardized academic report and presentation: Write a logically rigorous and format-standardized final report, deeply explaining parameter optimization laws and high-temperature degradation mechanisms. And make an academic report based on core research conclusions.

Simultaneous Multi-Wavelength Mode-Locked DFB Laser


1.      Background


Multi-wavelength mode-locked semiconductor lasers are essential for next-generation dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM) communications, coherent LiDAR, and high-resolution photonic sensing. Existing implementations often require multiple discrete single-wavelength lasers and complex integration schemes, leading to increased footprint, power consumption, and manufacturing cost. This project seeks to develop a compact, monolithically integrated multi-wavelength mode-locked laser leveraging waveguide Bragg gratings (WBGs) or four-phase-shifted chirped-sampled Bragg gratings (4PS-CSBGs). By generating multiple phase-locked wavelengths from a single chip, the proposed device will deliver enhanced stability, scalability, and manufacturability, paving the way for highly integrated photonic systems.


2. Main Tasks


  • Simulate the material and modal gain of a five-quantum-well epilayer using Photonic Integrated Circuit (PIC)group MATLAB codes.
  • Simulate near-field and far-field patterns using RSoft BeamPROP software.
  • Design a WBG microcavity or 4PS-CSBG laser supporting triple- and six-wavelength operation around 1.55 μm using PIC group MATLAB codes.
  • Simulate device behaviour (transmission spectrum, group delay, and photon density profile) using the Transfer Matrix Method (TMM) with PIC group tools.
  • Design the fabrication process and characterisation setup, including:
  • Optical spectral measurements (Optical spectrum analyser),
  • Pulse width measurements (autocorrelator),
  • Radio frequency (RF) stability characterisation (Electrical spectrum analyser).


3. Expected Outcomes


  • Demonstrate four types of multi-wavelength mode-locked DFB lasers with stable wavelengths within a single cavity and a consistent free spectral range (FSR) across a wide range of DFB currents and saturable absorber (SA) reverse voltages.
  • Achieve nearly transform-limited pulses with a time-bandwidth product approaching the Fourier transform limit.
  • Quantify the performance variations associated with cavity length and π-phase shifts.


4. Student Work Distribution


  • Student 1: Design of the laser cavity and WBG structure for triple-wavelength operation around 1.55 μm.
  • Student 2: Design of the laser cavity and WBG structure for six-wavelength operation around 1.55 μm.
  • Student 3: Design of the laser cavity and 4PS-CSBG structure for triple-wavelength operation around 1.55 μm.
  • Student 4: Design of the laser cavity and 4PS-CSBG structure for six-wavelength operation around 1.55 μm.

Reconfigurable Multi-Passband Microwave Photonic Filters


1.      Background


Microwave signal filtering is essential in RF systems. Leveraging integrated photonics, emerging microwave photonic filter (PF) platforms offer reconfigurable, widely tunable filtering with advantages in size, weight, stability, power efficiency, and latency—beyond

what conventional electronics can achieve. This project develops a compact, monolithically integrated filter using thermally-tuned conventional or four-phase-shift sampled Bragg gratings (C-SBG or 4PS-SBG) on the Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) platform. Through the Reconstruction Equivalent Chirp (REC) technique, the design enables channel independence, wide tunability, low insertion loss, high side-mode suppression ratio (SMSR), and fine spectral resolution.


2. Main Tasks


· Use Lumerical FDE to simulate material properties, waveguide dimensions, effective refractive index (nₑff), and optical confinement of on-chip ridge waveguides.


· Analyse electric field distributions for single- and multi-mode operations and identify critical conditions using Lumerical FDE.


· Design C-band dual- and four-passband PFs based on equivalent chirped C-SBG or 4PS-SBG structures.


· Simulate static performance (transmission spectra, photon distribution) using Lumerical FDTD and the Transfer Matrix Method (TMM).


· Model dynamic behaviour (neff, phase shift, spectral tuning vs. temperature) with Lumerical FDE, FDTD, COMSOL Multiphysics, and TMM.


· Develop the fabrication process flow and experimental characterisation setup.


3. Expected Outcomes


· Demonstrate four multi-channel PFs with tunable passbands, adjustable spacing, and a broad stopband range.


· Achieve SMSR > 10 dB.


· Ensure -3 dB bandwidth of all filtering windows < 20 GHz.


· Quantify static spectrum variations based on phase shift magnitude, number, and position.


4. Student Work Distribution

· Student 2: Design and Optimisation of a Dual-Channel Filter Cavity with Equivalent-Chirp 4PS-SBG at 1.55 μm

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

The BeiDou Navigation Satellite System has become a major enabling technology for positioning, navigation, timing, and intelligent applications in China and beyond. In recent years, low-altitude economy, intelligent transportation, unmanned systems, and infrastructure inspection have all created increasing demand for high-accuracy and high-reliability positioning solutions. In Hainan, this demand is particularly relevant due to the development of coastal transportation, island logistics, low-altitude UAV applications, and digital infrastructure management.

However, standalone BeiDou positioning performance may degrade in practical scenarios due to signal blockage, multipath, limited satellite visibility, atmospheric disturbances, and temporary interruptions. For intelligent inspection tasks using drones or mobile platforms, positioning continuity is as important as positioning accuracy. Integrating BeiDou with an inertial navigation system (INS) is a practical and widely adopted solution, where inertial sensing provides short-term continuity and GNSS provides long-term correction.

2. Main Task

This project aims to develop a BeiDou/INS integrated positioning method for low-altitude intelligent inspection applications. The student will first study the principles of BeiDou positioning, inertial sensor errors, coordinate systems, motion modeling, and data fusion algorithms. The project may use public GNSS/IMU datasets, simulation data, or small-scale experimental datadepending on resource availability.

The main technical work is to implement and evaluate a fusion algorithm based on Kalman Filter, Extended Kalman Filter, Unscented Kalman Filter, or equivalent sensor fusion schemes. The system should estimate position, velocity, and possibly attitude information, and compare the performance of standalone BeiDou, standalone INS dead reckoning, and integrated BeiDou/INS solutions. The student is encouraged to consider realistic scenarios such as partial signal blockage or short GNSS outages of 5–20 seconds.

Quantitative objectives may include reducing positioning error by at least 30% compared with standalone BeiDou under degraded signal conditions, maintaining continuous trajectory output during simulated outages, and achieving stable trajectory reconstruction in representative inspection scenarios.

3. Expected Outcomes

Expected outcomes include a BeiDou/INS positioning algorithm, a simulation or experimental evaluation platform, and a quantitative comparison of different positioning strategies. The final system should demonstrate improved accuracy, continuity, and robustness in low-altitude or mobile inspection scenarios. The dissertation should include theoretical modeling, algorithm implementation, trajectory analysis, and error statistics under multiple test conditions. This project is especially suitable for students interested in navigation, intelligent systems, low-altitude applications, and BeiDou-enabled engineering innovation.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Communication and navigation systems increasingly operate in dense and complex electromagnetic environments, where different forms of intentional or unintentional interference may significantly degrade system reliability and service quality. In wireless communication systems, interference may reduce throughput and increase bit error rate; in navigation systems, especially satellite-based systems such as BeiDou, interference may cause signal loss, tracking failure, or severe positioning degradation. Therefore, accurate recognition of interference types is an important prerequisite for adaptive anti-jamming and interference mitigation.

Traditional interference recognition methods typically rely on manually designed features derived from the spectrum, energy distribution, bandwidth, or statistical properties of the received signal. These methods are often limited when dealing with low signal-to-noise ratio, mixed interference, or highly dynamic signal environments. By combining time-frequency analysis with deep learning, interference recognition can be formulated as a data-driven pattern classification problem, allowing automatic extraction of discriminative features from spectrogram-like representations.

2. Main Task

This project aims to investigate intelligent recognition of communication/navigation interference signals using time-frequency analysis and deep learning techniques. The student will first model or simulate several representative interference types, such as single-tone interference, multi-tone interference, narrowband interference, broadband noise interference, chirp interference, pulsed interference, and sweep interference. A dataset containing around 5,000–15,000 signal samples under different SNR or JSR conditions is recommended.

The student will then generate time-frequency representations using methods such as Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), wavelet transform, or other suitable approaches, and compare their effectiveness. Based on these representations, a classifier using CNN, ResNet, MobileNet, Vision Transformer, or a hybrid deep network will be designed and trained. The project should compare multiple architectures and evaluate robustness under different noise levels, especially under low-SNR conditions.

Quantitative research targets may include classification accuracy of above 90% under moderate conditions and above 80% under low-SNR scenarios, together with clear confusion matrix analysis and robustness evaluation.

3. Expected Outcomes

Expected outcomes include a simulated interference dataset, a complete time-frequency feature extraction and classification pipeline, and a trained deep learning model for interference recognition. The final report should demonstrate the ability of the proposed method to distinguish multiple interference categories with satisfactory robustness. Evaluation should include accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, confusion matrix, and sensitivity to SNR/JSR variations. This topic is well aligned with the strengths of electronic information engineering, intelligent signal processing, and communication systems, and is particularly suitable for students considering postgraduate study in communications, signal processing, or navigation.
rows.themeTitle: Communication/Navigation Interference Signal Recognition Based on Time-Frequency Analysis and Deep Learning

1. Background

Roads and bridges are key components of modern transportation infrastructure, and their service safety is closely related to regular inspection and maintenance. Surface defects such as cracks, potholes, spalling, exposed reinforcement, and water seepage may gradually develop into serious structural problems if not identified at an early stage. Conventional manual inspection methods are often labor-intensive, subjective, slow, and difficult to scale, especially in large-area or hard-to-access scenarios. With recent advances in deep learning and computer vision, image-based automatic defect detection has become a highly promising approach for intelligent infrastructure inspection.

For Hainan and similar coastal or rapidly developing regions, the need for efficient transportation maintenance and digital infrastructure management is increasing. Therefore, a practical and lightweight AI-based detection system is of clear engineering relevance. Since deployment on mobile or edge devices is desirable in real applications, both detection accuracy and computational efficiency should be considered.

2. Main Task

This project aims to develop a lightweight deep learning framework for automatic detection and quantitative assessment of road and bridge surface defects. The student will first review common defect categories and prepare a labeled dataset using public data and/or self-collected images. A dataset of approximately 1,500–3,000 images covering at least 4–6 common defect typesis recommended. The project will then implement a baseline model using architectures such as YOLOv8, YOLOv10, RT-DETR, or lightweight segmentation networks, followed by optimization for small-target detection, robustness under illumination variation, and reduced model complexity.

Possible technical improvements include data augmentation, attention mechanisms, lightweight backbones, pruning, and feature fusion strategies. In addition to defect localization, the student is encouraged to explore basic quantitative indicators such as crack length, defect area, or severity level estimation. The target is to achieve mAP@0.5 above 80% , with an inference speed suitable for near real-time testing, e.g., above 15–20 FPS on a standard GPU platform.

3. Expected Outcomes

Expected outcomes include a defect image dataset, a trained lightweight detection model, a comparative evaluation against baseline methods, and a prototype interface for result visualization. The final system should be able to identify major surface defects and provide basic quantitative inspection outputs. The dissertation is expected to include model design, experimental validation, ablation studies, and performance comparison in terms of precision, recall, F1-score, mAP, inference speed, and model size. This project is suitable for students interested in AI, computer vision, and intelligent infrastructure applications.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Background:

UAV aerial images are widely used in smart transportation, urban monitoring, agriculture, emergency response, and remote sensing. Because UAV images are usually captured from high altitude and oblique viewpoints, the objects in the images are often small, densely distributed, partially occluded, and mixed with complex backgrounds. In this project, object detection clearly means recognizing and locating targets captured in UAV aerial images, such as vehicles, pedestrians, and other ground objects, rather than detecting the UAV itself. The main experimental dataset for this project is VisDrone2019, which will be used for model training, validation, testing, and comparison. YOLOv11 provides a strong one-stage detection framework with a good balance between accuracy and speed, making it suitable for object recognition and detection in UAV aerial images.


Main tasks:

1. Study the research status and development trend of object detection in UAV aerial images, especially small-object detection under complex backgrounds.

2. Analyze the basic architecture of YOLOv11, including its backbone, neck, detection head, feature extraction process, and inference workflow.

3. Build the experimental pipeline based on the VisDrone2019 dataset, including data preprocessing, annotation format conversion if needed, training configuration, validation, and testing.

4. Improve YOLOv11 according to the characteristics of UAV aerial images in VisDrone2019, focusing on small targets, dense targets, occlusion, scale changes, and complex scenes.

5. Design or optimize multi-scale feature fusion modules to improve the model's ability to detect objects of different sizes in UAV images.

6. Conduct experiments on VisDrone2019 and compare the improved method with YOLOv5, YOLOv7, the original YOLOv11, and other mainstream detection methods using metrics such as precision, recall, mAP, inference speed, parameter size, and computational cost.

7. Develop a visualization interface to demonstrate the complete workflow on UAV aerial images, including image upload or selection, YOLOv11 model inference, target box drawing, category recognition, confidence display, and final detection result output.


Expected outcomes:

The project is expected to improve YOLOv11 for recognizing and detecting targets in UAV aerial images, complete training and experimental comparison on the VisDrone2019 dataset, implement a visualization demo for the detection workflow, and write a graduation thesis explaining the model design, dataset processing, technical route, experiments, results, and conclusions.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Background:

Diffusion models have become an important class of generative models for image synthesis and image editing. Compared with traditional image processing methods, diffusion-based methods can follow text instructions, preserve visual realism, and support local or global modifications of image content. This project studies image editing methods based on diffusion models and focuses on understanding their principles, implementation workflow, evaluation methods, and practical prototype development.


Main tasks:

1. Understand the basic principles of generative diffusion models and their applications in image generation.

2. Master mainstream diffusion-model-based image editing methods, including text-guided editing, local editing, and global image modification.

3. Become familiar with mainstream deep learning frameworks and related diffusion model libraries.

4. Try to improve an existing image editing diffusion model, such as through prompt design, attention control, mask guidance, model component adjustment, or result post-processing.

5. Conduct comprehensive quantitative and qualitative analysis on benchmark datasets, and compare the proposed or improved method with existing advanced models.

6. Use methods such as attention map visualization to analyze how the model understands and associates text instructions with image regions, and explain the editing results.

7. Build a visualization interface to demonstrate the complete input-to-output workflow, including image input, text instruction input, editing process, and edited image output.


Expected outcomes:

The project is expected to design and implement a prototype system for image editing based on diffusion models. The system should modify local or global image content according to user-provided text instructions. The final outcomes include the prototype system, experimental comparison and analysis, visualization results, and a graduation thesis describing the design, implementation, experiments, and conclusions.

Background:

Relation extraction is an important information extraction task that identifies semantic relations between entities in text. Traditional supervised methods usually rely on labeled data and task-specific model training, while large language models provide new possibilities for relation extraction through instruction following, prompt design, in-context learning, and stronger semantic understanding. This project focuses on relation extraction methods based on large language models in open and public-domain scenarios.


Main tasks:

1. Learn the basic development workflow of deep learning and become familiar with commonly used frameworks such as PyTorch.

2. Review the development history of relation extraction, including rule-based methods, supervised learning methods, neural network methods, and recent large language model based methods.

3. Study the application and development trend of large language models in information extraction tasks, especially entity and relation extraction.

4. Design and implement a relation extraction method combined with large language models, and compare it with traditional supervised relation extraction methods.

5. Try to improve an existing LLM-based relation extraction method, such as through prompt optimization, output constraint design, or result post-processing, to improve extraction quality.

6. Conduct experiments on multiple public datasets, compare the performance of different models using metrics such as precision, recall, and F1 score, and analyze typical errors.

7. Develop a visualization interface to demonstrate the complete relation extraction workflow, including text input, entity recognition, relation extraction, and result display.


Expected outcomes:

The project is expected to deliver a working relation extraction system based on large language models, experimental comparison results on public datasets, a visualization demo, and a graduation thesis that explains the design process, model structure, experimental analysis, and conclusions.

1. Background

A patent for invention is a core intellectual property carrier for the protection of scientific and technological innovation achievements. After completing technical research and development, researchers usually have a complete technical report. However, most inventors lack standardized training in patent drafting and are unfamiliar with patent drafting rules such as claim layout and specification disclosure requirements, which easily leads to problems such as improper disclosure scope and blurred protection boundaries. This not only affects the grant success rate of patent applications, but also makes it difficult to effectively protect their own technical rights and interests.

In recent years, large language models and agent technologies have developed rapidly, providing new support for automated text generation and professional content creation. Facing the actual demand of transforming technological achievements into patent texts, this topic explores the realization of automatic conversion and drafting from technical reports to invention patent specifications based on large language models combined with agent architecture, so as to help improve the patent drafting efficiency and text quality of researchers.


2. Main task

1）Study the basic principles of large language models and the core theories of model fine-tuning methods, sort out the applicable fine-tuning schemes for professional text generation tasks in the patent field.

2）Learn the working principle of multi-agent collaboration technology, master the common construction methods of LLM-based multi-agent systems, and clarify the functional division logic of different agents.

3）Sort out the writing norms and conversion rules of invention patent documents, and complete the overall architecture design and code construction of the multi-agent patent writing system.

4）Optimize the prompting strategy and model parameters of each functional agent based on labeled patent data to improve the compliance and accuracy of generated patent texts.

5）Design a targeted test plan, conduct functional verification and effect evaluation on the developed system, and sort out existing problems and optimization directions.

6）Sort out the research content and experimental results, complete the writing of the graduation thesis in accordance with the standardized format requirements.


3. Expected outcomes

A working prototype of multi-agent based invention patent writing intelligent system, which can realize automatic conversion and auxiliary drafting from technical reports to standard invention patent specification, covering core sections such as specification text description and claims drafting.

A complete graduation thesis that sorts out the theoretical basis, system design, development process, experimental test results and conclusion analysis of the research, meeting the standardized format requirements of undergraduate graduation design.
rows.themeTitle: ‌Design and Implementation of an Intelligent Agent for Invention Patent Drafting Based on Large Language Models

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background


Network traffic measurement plays a fundamental role in modern network

management by providing essential traffic state information for tasks

such as anomaly detection, load balancing, and quality-of-service

assurance. However, due to the severely constrained memory and

computational resources of commodity switches, achieving fine-grained

and accurate traffic measurement at scale remains a significant

challenge. To improve measurement efficiency under resource constraints,

network-level collaborative measurement has emerged as a promising

approach. Rather than measuring all traffic independently at each

switch, measurement tasks are distributed across multiple switch nodes

in a coordinated manner, avoiding redundant monitoring of the same

flow and enabling each switch to focus on a distinct subset of

passing traffic. This collaborative paradigm improves both resource

utilization and measurement accuracy across the network. Nevertheless, the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of real-world

network traffic makes static task allocation strategies inadequate.

The measurement workload varies continuously across switches, and

suboptimal allocation decisions can lead to coverage gaps or resource

waste. This project addresses the dynamic allocation of collaborative

measurement tasks through a multi-agent reinforcement learning

framework, in which distributed switch agents learn to coordinate

their measurement strategies adaptively in response to evolving

traffic conditions, without requiring centralized control or

prior knowledge of traffic distributions.





2. Main task




（1）Study the fundamental principles of data center networks;




（2）Master widely used traffic measurement methods in data center networks;




（3）Learn typical reinforcement learning methods;




（4）Design a cooperative traffic measurement method based on muti-agent reinforcement learning algorithms;




（5）Perform simulation validation and continuous improvement of the proposed algorithm;




（6）Complete the undergraduate thesis.






3. Expected outcomes




(1) An intelligent system for cooperative network traffic measurement;




(2) An undergraduate thesis based on the research and implementation of the above system.
rows.themeTitle: ‌Research on Cooperative Network Traffic Measurement Mechanism Based on Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning

rows.themeProjectDescription: The concentration and particle size distribution of suspended particles in solution are important parameters for assessing water quality, pharmaceutical purity, and the quality of chemical liquids. This project aims to develop a rapid detection method based on the principle of light scattering. When a light beam passes through a solution containing particles, scattered light is generated at specific angles. The intensity of the scattered light is proportional to the particle concentration, while the angular distribution of the scattered light is related to the particle size. This research plans to design a miniature optical path system, using a laser light source and high-sensitivity photodetectors, to construct a portable detection device. By measuring the scattered light intensity and angular distribution, combined with inversion calculations based on the Mie scattering model, the project aims to achieve simultaneous quantitative analysis of particle concentration and size. This method requires no complex pretreatment, offers rapid response, and is non-contact and non-destructive. It is expected to provide an efficient, online tool for particle detection in environmental monitoring, the pharmaceutical industry, and process control.
rows.themeTitle: Measurement of Suspended Particles in Solution Using Light Scattering

rows.themeProjectDescription: Polymer optical waveguides hold significant application value in the fields of integrated photonics and optical interconnects. This project aims to develop a high-precision, rapid fabrication method for polymer optical waveguides by combining digital light processing (DLP) technology with a light-induced self-writing polymer process. Utilizing the high-resolution dynamic masking capability of DLP technology, a pre-designed patterned light beam is projected into a photosensitive polymer precursor solution. Localized photopolymerization is initiated by the light, enabling one-step self-writing formation of the waveguide structure, thereby avoiding the complex mask fabrication and development steps inherent in traditional photolithography. The study will systematically investigate the effects of exposure dosage, light intensity distribution, and polymer formulation on the waveguide geometry and optical performance, and will characterize key parameters such as propagation loss and mode coupling. This work aims to establish a flexible and efficient new strategy for polymer optical waveguide manufacturing, providing technical support for the development of on-chip optical interconnects, optical sensing, and flexible photonic devices.
rows.themeTitle: Fabrication of Light-Induced Self-Written Optical Waveguides Using DLP Technology
