rows.themeProjectDescription:
This project aims to design a high-input-impedance, low-noise active electrode circuit for biopotential sensing applications. Biopotential signals such as ECG, EEG, and EMG are typically weak, low-frequency, and easily affected by electrode-skin impedance, motion artifacts, power-line interference, and circuit noise. Therefore, the sensing front-end requires very high input impedance, low input-referred noise, sufficient gain, good common-mode rejection, and low power consumption.

The project will focus on the design and verification of an active electrode front-end circuit. The core circuit is a high-input-impedance input buffer that with low noise performance, and techniques such as positive feedback enhancing input impedance, capacitive coupling, pseudo-resistor-based high-pass filtering, chopper stabilization, or common-mode feedback maybe included. The target is to improve the signal quality at the electrode interface and reduce the influence of electrode impedance and external interference.

The main tasks include literature review, specification definition, circuit architecture design, transistor-level circuit implementation, simulation verification, and performance evaluation. Key performance metrics include input impedance, bandwidth, input-referred noise, power consumption, and robustness under process, voltage, and temperature variations.

Expected project outcomes include a complete circuit schematic, simulation results, performance comparison with existing designs, and a final technical report. For advanced students, layout design and post-layout simulation can be included for bonus consideration.
rows.themeTitle: Design of a High-Input-Impedance Low-Noise Active Electrode Circuit for Biopotential Sensing

Benefiting from its all-weather and all-day working capability, SAR has been widely applied in numerous fields including navigation, guidance, remote sensing, reconnaissance, and resource exploration. Nevertheless, SAR images lack intuitive color and structural reflection features of targets, which brings great difficulties to target identification. Accordingly, SAR image target classification has long been a challenging research task in the remote sensing field. In recent years, with the rapid advancement of deep learning techniques, deep network-based SAR image target recognition has become a prevailing research hotspot. This research aims to effectively improve the performance and efficiency of SAR target detection.

Background:

Forest fires are important ecological and environmental disturbances that can cause vegetation loss, biodiversity degradation, soil erosion, carbon emissions, and threats to human life and property. Sichuan Province has complex topography, diverse climate conditions, rich forest resources, and significant spatial differences in vegetation types and human activities. These factors make forest fire occurrence highly heterogeneous in both space and time. In recent years, climate variability, extreme weather events, land use change, and increasing human activities have further influenced forest fire risk. Understanding the spatiotemporal evolution characteristics of forest fires in Sichuan Province is therefore important for fire prevention, ecological protection, disaster risk management, and sustainable forest resource planning. Attribution analysis can help identify the key driving factors behind fire occurrence and provide scientific support for regional forest fire monitoring and early warning.

Main Task:

The main task of this project is to analyze the spatiotemporal distribution patterns and possible driving factors of forest fires in Sichuan Province. The student will first conduct a literature review on forest fire monitoring, spatial-temporal pattern analysis, and fire attribution methods. Then, forest fire occurrence data will be collected and organized, which may include satellite fire point products, burned area datasets, meteorological data, vegetation indices, topographic data, land use data, and human activity indicators. Data preprocessing may include coordinate transformation, spatial matching, temporal aggregation, missing value processing, and construction of analysis units. Based on these datasets, the student will analyze the temporal variation of forest fires at annual, seasonal, and monthly scales, and investigate spatial clustering, hotspot distribution, and regional differences. Furthermore, attribution analysis will be conducted to explore the influence of factors such as temperature, precipitation, wind speed, humidity, elevation, slope, vegetation coverage, land use type, population density, and distance to roads or settlements. Possible methods include correlation analysis, regression models, random forest, geographic detector, or spatial statistical methods.

Expected Outcome:

The expected outcome of this project includes a structured forest fire dataset for Sichuan Province, a set of spatiotemporal analysis results, attribution analysis of major driving factors, source code or GIS workflows, and visualized maps and charts. The student is expected to reveal the temporal trends, seasonal characteristics, spatial hotspots, and regional differences of forest fires in Sichuan Province. The project should identify the key natural and human-related factors associated with forest fire occurrence and explain their possible mechanisms. The final results may provide useful reference for forest fire prevention, risk zoning, ecological management, and disaster mitigation. Through this project, the student will gain practical experience in remote sensing data processing, GIS spatial analysis, environmental data integration, statistical modeling, and scientific thesis writing.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1 Background

State Space Models (SSMs), particularly Mamba, have emerged as a compelling alternative to Transformers, offering linear computational complexity in long-sequence modeling while maintaining competitive performance. However, the growing parameter sizes of SSMs create significant deployment challenges on resource-constrained edge devices. Model compression techniques—structured pruning, quantization, and low-rank decomposition—are essential for lightweight deployment, but they introduce complex trade-offs among compression ratio, inference speed, accuracy retention, and hardware energy efficiency. Traditional single-objective compression approaches fail to capture these competing demands. Multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) such as NSGA-II and MOEA/D provide a principled framework for navigating these trade-offs by generating Pareto-optimal solution sets. Furthermore, assessing compression strategies solely on GPU metrics overlooks the energy efficiency characteristics of emerging compute-in-memory (CIM) accelerators, which are critical for embodied AI applications. CIM-MLC (architecture-level) and NeuroSim (circuit-level) are two complementary simulation tools for CIM energy estimation.

2 Main Task

This project develops an automated multi-objective compression framework for SSMs that jointly optimizes four objectives:

(i) model compression ratio,

(ii) inference throughput,

(iii) accuracy retention on downstream tasks, and

(iv) energy efficiency on CIM simulators.

The student will first survey SSM architectures (Mamba, Mamba2) and compression methodologies. Then, a modular compression pipeline will be implemented, supporting structured pruning, INT8/FP16 quantization, and low-rank factorization. NSGA-II and MOEA/D will be integrated to search the high-dimensional configuration space, with Pareto front convergence analysis across algorithms. Critically, compressed models will be evaluated not only on standard benchmarks (e.g., long-range arena) but also on CIM simulators to quantify actual energy-performance trade-offs. The primary evaluation tool is CIM-MLC; NeuroSim can be used as an alternative circuit-level estimator.

Tasks

• Survey SSM architecture fundamentals (Mamba, Mamba2) and existing model compression techniques

• Formulate SSM compression as a multi-objective optimization problem (compression ratio vs. accuracy vs. speed vs. energy)

• Implement a compression evaluation pipeline supporting pruning, quantization, and low-rank decomposition

• Apply NSGA-II and MOEA/D to search optimal compression configurations and compare their Pareto fronts

• Evaluate compressed SSM models on long-sequence benchmarks and CIM simulators (CIM-MLC primary, NeuroSim alternative) for energy-performance trade-offs

• Compare SSM compression Pareto fronts against Transformer compression to analyze architectural advantages

3 Expected Outcomes

The project will deliver:

(a) a comparative analysis of Pareto fronts achieved by different MOEAs for SSM compression;

(b) an open-source compression-evaluation toolkit integrating CIM-MLC (with NeuroSim as alternative) for energy modeling;

(c) empirical guidelines for selecting compression strategies based on deployment constraints; and

(d) validation that multi-objective optimization outperforms single-objective baselines in balancing accuracy-efficiency trade-offs.

Results may contribute to a conference submission or technical report.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Multi-unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems are required to perform full-coverage scanning over extensive target areas for missions such as border patrol, post-disaster area assessment and large-scale farm monitoring. In practical operations, UAVs are subject to multiple constraints, including limited communication bandwidth caused by signal attenuation and interference, restricted communication range that may lead to disconnection beyond effective coverage, as well as battery capacity limitations characterized by short endurance and mandatory return for recharging. Traditional coverage planning methods generally assume ideal communication conditions and unlimited energy supply, which often results in communication outages or power depletion during actual flight. It remains a challenging task to achieve complete area coverage via cooperative planning of multiple UAVs under dual constraints of communication and energy, while minimizing total energy consumption and flight duration. This project investigates cooperative coverage planning strategies for multi-UAV systems with communication and energy limitations, aiming to enhance the robustness and practicality of the overall system. The main research tasks are specified as follows:

1) Constraint Modeling and Problem Formalization

Establish UAV communication range models, signal attenuation models (e.g., free-space path loss model) and energy consumption models correlated with flight speed, travel distance and payload. Formulate communication connectivity constraints requiring each UAV to maintain connection with at least one in-range UAV, and energy feasibility constraints stipulating that the total energy consumption of flight paths shall not exceed battery capacity. The cooperative coverage planning problem is ultimately formalized as a constrained combinatorial optimization problem.

2) Area Decomposition and Coverage PathGeneration

Propose an area decomposition approach based on grid graphs or Voronoi diagrams to partition the large target region into multiple subregions and assign each subregion to individual UAVs. For each divided subregion, generate global coverage paths adopting Boustrophedon scanning or spiral coverage patterns. The number of turns is further optimized to reduce overall energy consumption.

3) Communication Relay and Energy Coordination Strategy

Develop an inter-UAV communication relay mechanism. When a UAV suffers weak signals due to excessive distance from the base station, another UAV will be dynamically scheduled as a relay node to sustain the connectivity of the entire UAV swarm. Meanwhile, an energy-balanced task scheduling scheme is designed to assign more coverage tasks to UAVs with sufficient remaining power, so as to prevent early return of individual UAVs.

4) Simulation Validation and Performance Evaluation

Construct a large-scale outdoor simulation environment with undulating terrain sized at 500 m × 500 m using Gazebo or AirSim, where 3 to 5 quadrotor UAVs are deployed. Comparative experiments are conducted against classic coverage planning without constraint consideration, schemes with only energy constraints and schemes with only communication constraints. Evaluation metrics include full coverage rate, maximum variance of energy consumption, number of communication interruptions and total mission time. A visualization interface is also developed to display real-time communication link status and residual energy during cooperative coverage operations.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
After the occurrence of natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods and wildfires, cooperative search and rescue (SAR) with multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can rapidly cover large-scale complex terrains and improve the efficiency of survivor detection. Nevertheless, the SAR environment presents

multiple challenges, including uneven distribution of mission points, limited endurance of UAVs, dynamically changing communication topologies, and time-decaying mission values. These characteristics render traditional task allocation methods incapable of real-time adaptation to dynamic scenarios. Moreover, such methods lack the capability to structurally model the complex interactions among agents, thus failing to achieve real-time and efficient task allocation. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can effectively represent the heterogeneous relational graph between UAVs and missions, and learn optimal allocation strategies by exploiting topological information. Accordingly, this project leverages the representation learning capability of GNNs for non-Euclidean data to investigate multi-UAV task allocation methods tailored for SAR scenarios, aiming to maximize overall search-and-rescue benefits and minimize mission completion time. The main research contents are outlined as follows:

1) SAR Scenario Modeling and Graph Construction

Formulate the multi-UAV SAR task allocation problem in a formal manner. UAVs and mission points are defined as two types of nodes in a heterogeneous graph. Edge features incorporate the distance from UAVs to mission points, mission priority, time window constraints and communication topological relationships.

A dynamic task allocation model is established based on Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (Dec-POMDP).

2) Design of GNN-based Allocation Strategy

Develop a task allocation decision module based on Graph Attention Networks (GAT) or Graph Isomorphism Networks (GIN). Features of neighboring UAVs and missions are aggregated via message passing to output the allocation probability or marginal benefit of each UAV for individual missions. The Hungarian algorithm or greedy matching is adopted to convert probability outputs into feasible task allocation schemes.

3) Online Reallocation Mechanism for Dynamic Environments

To address dynamic events during SAR operations, including newly detected missions, UAV malfunctions and return-to-base for recharging, an incremental GNN-based task reallocation approach is proposed. By exploiting the locality of graph topology, only the embeddings of affected nodes are updated, so as to realize

low-latency online re-planning.

4) Simulation Verification and Performance Comparison

Construct SAR simulation environments based on AirSim or ROS combined with Gazebo, which cover terrains with obstacles, 10 to 20 mission points and 3 to 5 UAVs. Comparative experiments are conducted against classic greedy allocation, the Hungarian algorithm and reinforcement learning-based allocation methods. The

performance of the proposed method is evaluated in terms of mission completion rate, total flight distance and reallocation response time. Meanwhile, a visualization interface is developed to dynamically display the allocation graph and UAV flight paths during the whole process.
rows.themeTitle: Graph neural network based task allocation method for multi-UAV search and rescue missions

rows.themeProjectDescription:
In advanced packaging systems, excessive temperature can reduce device reliability, accelerate material degradation, increase thermal stress, and affect the long-term performance of interconnects. Therefore, effective heat dissipation design for glass-based packaging substrates is becoming an important research topic. One possible solution is to introduce microchannels into glass substrates, allowing coolant or working fluid to flow through the substrate and remove heat directly from the heat-generating area. Glass-based microfluidic cooling structures have the potential to combine electrical insulation, optical transparency, chemical resistance, and embedded thermal management in one platform.


The main tasks of this project are as follows:

Design one or more glass-based microchannel structures, such as straight channels, parallel channels, serpentine channels, or inlet–outlet manifold structures.

Define the key geometrical parameters of the microchannels, including channel width, depth, length, spacing, inlet/outlet diameter, and overall substrate size.

Analyze the effects of flow rate, channel size, channel layout, and heat flux on temperature distribution, maximum temperature, pressure drop, and cooling uniformity.

Discuss the possible fabrication routes for glass-based microchannels, such as wet etching, laser processing, mechanical micromachining, and glass bonding.


By the end of the project, the student is expected to achieve the following outcomes:

A clear understanding of the thermal management challenges of glass substrates in advanced packaging applications.

A complete design of a glass-based microchannel cooling structure, including layout drawings and key dimensional parameters.

A simulation model for analyzing fluid flow and heat transfer in the microchannel structure.

Quantitative results showing the relationship between channel geometry, flow rate, pressure drop, and cooling performance.

A possible final deliverable is a glass-based microchannel cooling design capable of reducing the peak substrate temperature by a measurable amount under a defined heat flux, while keeping the pressure drop within a practical operating range.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Emotion recognition is the core research direction in the field of affective computing, which has important application prospects in mental health monitoring and personalized medical services. Traditional emotion recognition methods mainly rely on external manifestations such as facial expressions and voice signals, which are easily interfered by subjective factors such as facial masking and emotional disguise, resulting in limited recognition accuracy and poor robustness. Physiological signals such as EEG (Electroencephalogram), ECG (Electrocardiogram) and GSR (Galvanic Skin Response) can objectively reflect the internal emotional changes of the human body without being affected by subjective disguise, and have become reliable data sources for high-precision emotion recognition. With the rapid development of multi-modal feature fusion and lightweight deep learning technologies, researches on feature alignment, heterogeneous data fusion and emotion classification based on multi-modal physiological signals have gradually become a hot spot. Existing studies have verified that combining EEG, ECG and GSR signals can significantly improve the generalization ability of emotion recognition models. However, there are still problems such as signal heterogeneity, redundant feature information, large model parameters and difficulty in balancing accuracy and inference speed. This topic relies on public datasets AMIGOS and ASCERTAIN, aiming to design a lightweight emotion recognition algorithm integrating cross-modal feature alignment and context perception. By optimizing the preprocessing workflow, feature fusion strategy and network architecture, this method can effectively solve the problems of inconsistent modal distribution and excessive model complexity.


References

[1].Wang, X., Zhang, J., He, C., Wu, H., & Cheng, L. (2023). A novel emotion recognition method based on the feature fusion of single-lead EEG and ECG signals. IEEE Internet of Things Journal, 11(5), 8746-8756.

[2].JJoshi, S., & Srinivas, L. N. B. (2025). An ensemble classifier for emotion classification from EEG and GSR signals for autism detection. Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine, 270, 108921.

[3].Xu, Z., Chen, N., Li, G., Li, J., Zhu, H., & Zhu, Z. (2025). Emotion recognition based on time-scale heterogeneity and hierarchical spatial coupling analysis of multimodal physiological signals. Expert Systems with Applications, 285, 128035.

[4].Xu, Z., Chen, N., Li, G., Li, J., Zhu, H., & Zhu, Z. (2025). Emotion recognition based on time-scale heterogeneity and hierarchical spatial coupling analysis of multimodal physiological signals. Expert Systems with Applications, 285, 128035.

[5].Li, G., Chen, N., Zhu, H., Li, J., Xu, Z., & Zhu, Z. (2025). Uncertainty-Aware Graph Contrastive Fusion Network for multimodal physiological signal emotion recognition. Neural

Networks, 187, 107363.


2. Main Tasks


1. Multimodal physiological signal preprocessing and feature engineering: Preprocess multimodal physiological signals including electroencephalogram (EEG), electrocardiogram (ECG) and galvanic skin response (GSR), and then conduct multi-dimensional feature extraction, so as to provide a solid data foundation for subsequent model analysis.

2. Cross-modal feature alignment and fusion model: Integrate feature alignment algorithms with signal fusion strategies to unify the representation forms of heterogeneous multimodal data. Meanwhile, construct a lightweight network architecture to balance recognition accuracy and model structural compactness.

3. Algorithm optimization and evaluation: Optimize and iterate the model by adopting network pruning and other lightweight methods. Multiple evaluation metrics are adopted to comprehensively assess the overall performance of the model. Finally, a series of comparative experiments are carried out to analyze the inference speed of different models and complete the performance verification of the overall algorithm.


3.Expected Outcomes

(1) A complete set of multi-modal physiological signal preprocessing and feature extraction code library.

(2) A lightweight emotion recognition model with classification accuracy ≥75%.

(3) Algorithm performance optimization analysis report and graduation thesis.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Project Background & Motivation

Face recognition technology has become widely used in areas such as access control, smart security, and human-computer interaction. However, implementing face recognition on embedded platforms often faces challenges including high computational complexity, limited hardware resources, and real-time performance constraints. This project aims to design a lightweight face recognition module based on an ARM processor combined with custom IP acceleration cores, and to verify the design on an FPGA platform. By offloading computation-intensive tasks to hardware accelerators, the system achieves both flexibility (via ARM software) and high performance (via hardware acceleration).


Project Objectives:

1. Design a complete face recognition module integrating image acquisition, preprocessing, feature extraction, and recognition.

2. Develop an ARM-based embedded software framework to control the recognition flow.

3. Design dedicated IP acceleration cores for key tasks (e.g., feature extraction or similarity computation) using HDL (Verilog/VHDL).

4. Integrate the ARM processor and IP cores into an FPGA-based SoC system.

5. Verify the functionality, performance, and resource utilization of the system on an FPGA development board (e.g., Xilinx Zynq series).


Expected Outcomes:

1.A functionally verified face recognition module on FPGA.

2.Source code for ARM embedded software and IP cores (Verilog/VHDL).

3.System block diagram, simulation waveforms, and on-board testing results.

4.Final project report and presentation.

rows.themeProjectDescription: Data prediction is a method that uses existing data to estimate future values, widely applied in processing multidimensional time series across fields such as finance, climate, and environment, and can be used to address issues like data compression and signal processing. This project focuses on time-series data collected from industrial sensors, investigating machine learning-based prediction methods. First, statistical analysis of the sample data is conducted to extract local features and segment the data accordingly. Next, each segment is classified to determine its type of variation. Then, a machine learning model is established and trained for each segment. Finally, the predictive models are tested and optimized using actual data, aiming to achieve optimal prediction accuracy.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

The rapid growth of large-model training, high-performance computing, and distributed storage has placed unprecedented stress on data center networks. Traditional protocols such as TCP/IP and static traffic scheduling policies struggle to satisfy microsecond-level latency requirements and hundred-gigabit throughput demands. AI training in particular generates synchronized burst traffic patterns that can rapidly overflow switch buffers, leading to packet loss and timeout-triggered retransmissions that are catastrophic for latency-sensitive distributed workloads. While loss-less networking technologies such as RoCE with PFC alleviate some of these issues, they introduce new problems including head-of-line blocking, congestion spreading, and even deadlocks. Consequently, intelligent path selection, end-to-end congestion control, and active queue management at switches have become central research topics in both academia and industry.



2. Main Task

This project requires the student to design and implement a complete network transmission control framework within a high-fidelity discrete-event simulation environment. The student must take full control of three categories of strategies. First, on the sender side, the student will implement multi-flow scheduling, congestion window management, packet segmentation, retransmission queues, and timer-driven timeout handling. Second, on the receiver side, the student will design reordering buffers, selective acknowledgement (SACK) generation, delayed ACK strategies, and buffer-overflow-aware feedback to the sender. Third, at the switch nodes, the student will implement multi-path routing decisions (e.g., ECMP, congestion-aware routing, packet spraying), priority-based queue scheduling, and AQM-style proactive dropping policies. All control logic must operate in a fully distributed manner, exchanging information solely through in-band packet fields, since no centralized controller or shared memory is available. The implementation must respect physical constraints such as link bandwidth limits, propagation delay, finite switch buffer capacity, and receiver memory limits.



3. Expected Outcomes

Upon completion, the student is expected to deliver:

(1) a fully functional Python implementation conforming to the interface, capable of guaranteeing in-order, lossless delivery of all flows across multiple benchmark datasets;

(2) a comparative evaluation of at least three congestion control variants and two multi-path routing strategies, measured in terms of flow completion time, throughput, deadline-miss rate, and final composite score defined by the contest scoring rule (weighted flow score multiplied by squared completion ratio);

(3) a thesis document including a literature review, system architecture diagrams, algorithmic pseudocode, experimental results with visualizations, and a critical discussion of trade-offs between fairness, latency, and throughput; and

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1) Organic mixed ionic-electronic conductors (OMIECs) are central to organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) and bioelectronics, where their swelling during ionic doping/dedoping critically influences device performance and stability. Existing techniques such as EQCM-D, AFM, and GIWAXS suffer from limited temporal/spatial resolution, inability for in-situ dynamic monitoring, or operational complexity. Recently, a high-resolution, real-time swelling-monitoring tool was developed in our lab, based on a customized laser Doppler vibrometer with mapping capability (LDV‑M).

The LDV‑M platform has enabled real‑time, high‑resolution mapping of swelling in OMIEC channels in conventional electrolytes (e.g., PBS). However, emerging electrolytes such as ionic liquids, hydrogel electrolytes, and bio‑inspired fluids exhibit unknown swelling behaviors due to their varied ion sizes, viscosities, and degrees of hydration. Understanding how these electrolytes dynamically affect OMIEC swelling is critical for developing next‑generation bioelectronics, neuromorphic devices, and implantable sensors. Yet, systematic monitoring of swelling across different electrolyte compositions remains unexplored.

2) This project will employ the established LDV‑M system to perform operando swelling monitoring of OMIEC channels in a series of emerging electrolytes, including ionic liquids, concentrated polymer electrolytes, etc. The study will map spatiotemporal swelling responses under varying gate frequencies, voltages, and cycling conditions. Key tasks include quantifying the magnitude of electrolyte‑dependent swelling, identifying transient ionic injection pathways, and correlating swelling behavior with device electrical performance and stability.

3) We expect to obtain comprehensive swelling‑electrolyte databases, revealing how ion species, mobility, and solvation affect OMIEC swelling kinetics and heterogeneity. The results will identify electrolytes that minimize parasitic swelling while maintaining high ionic conductivity, enabling more stable OECT operation.
rows.themeTitle: Swell Monitoring of Organic Mixied Ionic-Electronic Conductor in Emerging Electrolytes

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Human Activity Recognition (HAR) is a fundamental task in computer vision and intelligent perception, with broad applications in smart surveillance, human-computer interaction, and autonomous driving. This task aims to automatically identify and classify human behavior actions from visual or sensor data, providing perceptual intelligence for downstream decision-making. However, two major challenges remain in practical deployment: First, single-modality data (e.g., RGB images alone or point clouds alone) cannot simultaneously capture both appearance details and spatial structural information of human actions, leading to significant performance degradation under viewpoint changes and lighting variations. Second, existing multi-modal fusion methods typically rely on heavyweight architectures and large-scale annotated datasets, making them difficult to deploy on edge devices or real-time systems.

This project aims to leverage heterogeneous modality data fusion to achieve efficient and robust human activity recognition. The main contents include: 1. Theoretical foundations of heterogeneous data alignment and feature extraction from 2D (optical images) and 3D (radar point clouds/depth maps) modalities; 2. Designing a cross-modal fusion network that effectively integrates appearance features from 2D images with geometric features from 3D data; 3. Applying lightweight techniques to the fusion network to meet real-time inference requirements.

The anticipated project deliverables include: 1. A heterogeneous modality fusion network architecture for HAR; 2. Computer simulation results on public benchmark datasets; 3. Undergraduate thesis.

You can choose one or more programming languages such as C, C++, Python or MATLAB to realize your algorithms.
rows.themeTitle: Lightweight Human Activity Recognition Method Based on Heterogeneous Modality Data Fusion
